evidence.claim: A rock-covered water tower helped turn Jim Bishop’s planned family cottage into a castle.
evidence.quote: When Bishop got a water tower he decided to cover it with rocks. Several neighbors said it reminded them of a castle and Bishop noted it looked like a turret.

evidence.claim: Construction began in 1969 on land he had bought for $450 at age 15.
evidence.quote: Bishop bought the land for the site for $450 when he was 15, and construction on what was originally intended to be a family project to build a cottage started in 1969.

evidence.claim: Neighbors saw a castle in the tower, and Bishop took up the idea.
evidence.quote: Bishop took this into consideration and soon began building.

evidence.claim: His project became a roadside attraction on SH 165 in the Wet Mountains.
evidence.quote: The "castle" is located in south central Colorado, on State Highway 165, in the Wet Mountains of Southern Colorado

evidence.claim: A 1996 dispute over unauthorized signs ended with officials issuing road signs pointing to the site.

Cache contains little construction or campaigning history for the numbered roads. Overview history covers documented corridor use and designation without equating historic trails to today’s highways.
Material starts at Westcliffe. Moments run Westcliffe, Silver Cliff, then Bishop Castle on the southern branch. Pueblo is the other branch endpoint, not an intermediate point before Bishop Castle.
CDOT gives 3.5 hours; archived FHWA gives two hours. Current CDOT estimate used with attribution. Catalog mapped mileage (89.6) differs from CDOT’s designated 103 miles.
Observatory structure is described in Wikipedia as an old period building but also as built in 2015. Age claim and unverified free-access promise omitted; roof and telescope retained.
Westcliffe’s Wikipedia history calls the 1881 railroad Denver and Rio Grande Western; no underlying railway source is cached to distinguish company and successor. Railroad origin detail omitted.
